qs.q: Which statement concerning systemic manifestations of mumps virus infection is accurate?
o: The testes, ovaries and pancreas can be involved
Passive immunization is the sole means of disease prevention
There is no effective vaccine available against mumps
Laboratory cell culture isolation is required for all diagnoses
qs.e: Mumps complications can include orchitis, oophoritis, and pancreatitis, in addition to parotitis. An effective vaccine exists, and diagnosis relies on various laboratory methods beyond just culture.

qs.q: Mumps meningoencephalitis is typically mild, but damage to which cranial nerve can result in permanent deafness?
qs.e: Mumps meningoencephalitis is usually mild, but damage specifically to the 8th cranial nerve can lead to deafness. Other cranial nerves are less commonly associated with this specific complication.

qs.q: A 6-year-old child presents with tender, bilateral parotid gland swelling and fever. Why does infection with mumps virus confer lifelong immunity without second episodes?
o: Neutralizing antibody levels wane within six months
The causative organism exists as a single serotype
The viral genome undergoes rapid antigenic variation
qs.e: Mumps virus exists as only one serotype, meaning infection confers permanent immunity against reinfection. Organisms undergoing antigenic variation can cause recurrent infections.
qs.s: Medical Virology: Adenoviruses, Hemorrhagic Fever & Viral Receptors: MCQs

qs.q: Which clinical manifestation is a well-known complication associated with mumps virus infection?
o: Infection of testes, ovaries, and pancreas
qs.e: Mumps virus has a strong tropism for glandular tissues and can cause inflammation in the testes, ovaries, and pancreas. It is distinct from enteroviruses that cause hemorrhagic conjunctivitis or myocarditis.
qs.s: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) Guide: Pathogenesis, Dx & Treatment: MCQs

qs.q: A 30-year-old man is evaluated for infertility and a history of childhood mumps infection complicated by orchitis. Which microscopic change is most characteristic of the severe sequelae of mumps orchitis in adults?
o: Presence of intratubular germ cell neoplasia
Presence of tubular atrophy and fibrosis
qs.e: Mumps orchitis involves a lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate that can lead to severe necrosis, tubular atrophy, fibrosis, and subsequent sterility. Caseous granulomatous inflammation is characteristic of tuberculous epididymo-orchitis.
qs.s: Penile & Testicular Pathologies: Hypospadias, Tumors, Torsion – Male: MCQs

qs.q: An adult patient presents with painful enlargement of both parotid glands, associated with low-grade fever and malaise. The clinician suspects mumps sialadenitis. Which extra-salivary complication in adult males carries a risk of permanent sterility?
qs.e: In adults, mumps can cause pancreatitis or orchitis, with orchitis sometimes leading to sterility. Pancreatitis is another complication, but it does not directly cause sterility like testicular inflammation does.

qs.q: What is the body's target site for the paramyxovirus that causes mumps?
qs.e: Mumps virus primarily targets the parotid glands, causing characteristic swelling. It can also affect other glandular tissues like testes, ovaries, and pancreas.
qs.s: Weekly Year 3: Medical Virology Exam - October 16, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: Which one of the following statements concerning mumps is CORRECT?
o: Orchitis is a common complication in post-pubertal males.
It is primarily transmitted through contaminated food.
It is caused by a DNA virus.
A vaccine is not available for mumps.
qs.e: Orchitis (inflammation of the testes) is a common and painful complication of mumps in post-pubertal males. Mumps is caused by an RNA virus (paramyxovirus), a vaccine is available (MMR), and it's transmitted via respiratory droplets.
qs.s: Weekly Year 3: Medical Virology Exam - October 16, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

ai.title: Mumps (Paramyxovirus Infection)
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: Mumps is a contagious viral infection causing parotid swelling, orchitis, meningitis and pancreatitis. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by serology or PCR when available. Management is supportive; complications require prompt recognition.

sections.p: Mumps is an acute, self‑limited infection caused by the mumps virus, a paramyxovirus. It presents with fever and painful swelling of the parotid glands. Diagnosis is clinical; confirm with serum IgM or PCR if testing exists.
b: Parotid swelling is usually bilateral but may be unilateral.
Fever >38 °C often precedes glandular pain.

t.a: Serum IgM or PCR for mumps RNA
t.b: Confirms viral aetiology when the clinical picture is atypical; positive result supports diagnosis, negative does not rule out early infection.
Shows enlarged, hypoechoic gland with increased vascularity; helps differentiate from bacterial sialadenitis when imaging is limited.

sections.p: Mumps is usually mild, but complications define severity. Staging is pragmatic:
b: Stage 1 – Isolated parotitis, no systemic signs.
Stage 2 – Parotitis with fever, mild leukocytosis.
Stage 3 – Complications (orchitis, meningitis, pancreatitis, encephalitis).

sections.p: The primary cause is infection with the mumps virus. In low‑resource settings, co‑infection or mis‑diagnosis with other tropical viruses is common.
b: Mumps virus – most common worldwide.
Coxsackievirus – can mimic parotitis.
EBV or CMV – cause lymphadenopathy and fever.
Bacterial sialadenitis – secondary infection, especially in malnourished children.

sections.p: Typical presentation follows a 2‑ to 3‑day prodrome of low‑grade fever, malaise and headache, then painful swelling of one or both parotid glands.
b: Swelling begins at the angle of the jaw and may extend to the neck.
Unilateral orchitis in post‑pubertal males (≈30 % of cases).
Meningitis signs (photophobia, neck stiffness) in <1 % of children.
Pancreatitis – epigastric pain, vomiting, elevated amylase.

sections.p: Select investigations that answer a specific clinical question; if unavailable, rely on clinical judgement.

t.b: Detects leukocytosis (>12 × 10⁹/L) suggesting bacterial superinfection; normal or mild rise supports viral aetiology.
Elevated (>2 × upper limit) indicates pancreatitis, a recognised mumps complication.
CSF pleocytosis with lymphocyte predominance confirms viral meningitis; PCR for mumps if lab available.
Shows enlarged, hypoechoic testis; helps differentiate from torsion when surgical facilities are limited.

sections.p: Complications are uncommon but can be life‑threatening; recognise them early.
b: Encephalitis – altered consciousness, seizures.
Severe orchitis – testicular atrophy, infertility risk.
Acute pancreatitis – persistent vomiting, epigastric tenderness.
Meningitis – neck stiffness, photophobia.

sections.p: There is no specific antiviral; treatment is supportive and complication‑directed.
b: Analgesia/antipyretics – paracetamol or ibuprofen for pain and fever.
Hydration – oral fluids; IV if unable to tolerate.
Warm compresses to parotid region.
If bacterial superinfection suspected, start amoxicillin‑clavulanate (avoid if allergy).
Orchitis – scrotal support, NSAIDs; refer if testicular swelling >5 days.
Meningitis – admit, monitor, consider empirical ceftriaxone if bacterial meningitis cannot be excluded.

sections.p: Most children recover within 2 weeks. Follow‑up focuses on complications and vaccination status.
b: Re‑examine parotid swelling after 7 days; persistent pain warrants imaging.
Check testicular size in post‑pubertal males at 1‑month.
Ensure two‑dose MMR vaccination (first dose at 9 months, second at 15 months) per WHO schedule.
Educate families on droplet precautions for 5 days after symptom onset.

sections.p: Several conditions mimic mumps in low‑resource settings.
b: Bacterial sialadenitis – purulent discharge, high neutrophil count.
Parotid tumour – firm, non‑tender mass, progressive over weeks.
EBV infectious mononucleosis – cervical lymphadenopathy, atypical lymphocytes.
Coxsackievirus infection – hand‑foot‑mouth lesions, vesicular rash.

sections.p: Laboratory and clinical findings may be deceptive.
b: Normal leukocyte count does not exclude bacterial superinfection early.
Serum amylase may rise from salivary gland inflammation, not pancreatitis.
PCR may be negative if specimen taken >7 days after onset.

whenToSeekHelp: Unilateral testicular pain with swelling (rule out torsion).
Vomiting with epigastric pain and high amylase (pancreatitis).

faq.q: Is mumps still common where the MMR vaccine is used?
faq.a: Outbreaks occur in pockets of low vaccine coverage; in fully immunised populations it is rare.
No; they are only used for secondary bacterial infection.
The virus can inflame the eighth cranial nerve, leading to sensorineural hearing loss, usually temporary.

exam: A 6‑year‑old presents with unilateral parotid swelling and fever; what is your next diagnostic step — assess for bacterial superinfection with CBC and consider bedside ultrasound.
How would you differentiate mumps orchitis from testicular torsion in a 15‑year‑old — focus on gradual onset, pain relief with NSAIDs, and ultrasound findings.
A child with mumps develops neck stiffness; what investigations are indicated and why — perform lumbar puncture for CSF analysis to rule out meningitis.
Explain why amoxicillin‑clavulanate is chosen for suspected bacterial sialadenitis but not for uncomplicated mumps — it targets common oral flora and is unnecessary for viral disease.
What are the red‑flag signs that require urgent referral in a patient with mumps — encephalitis, severe orchitis, pancreatitis, or persistent high fever.
Discuss the public‑health measures to prevent mumps outbreaks in low‑resource settings — high‑coverage MMR vaccination, isolation for 5 days after symptom onset, community education.
Why might serum amylase be elevated in mumps without pancreatitis — salivary gland inflammation releases amylase; correlate with clinical picture and imaging.
A teenager with mumps reports hearing loss; what is the likely mechanism and management — viral inflammation of the eighth nerve; monitor, refer to audiology, steroids only in severe cases.
